<?php
/**
 * Reset the test content in ONE request.
 *
 * The contract suite re-seeds before every test to keep them isolated. Doing
 * that over REST cost a listing, a DELETE per existing page and a POST per
 * fixture — about thirteen sequential round trips against single-threaded
 * PHP-WASM, roughly ten seconds, times sixty-odd tests. That was the whole of
 * the seventeen-minute run; no adapter change moved it, because none of it was
 * adapter work.
 *
 * The documents arrive in the request body from seed.json, so this file never
 * becomes a second definition of what the fixture content is.
 */
add_action('rest_api_init', function () {

  register_rest_route('hydra-test/v1', '/reset', array(
    'methods' => 'POST',
    'permission_callback' => function ($request) {
      // Cookie auth for the REST API needs a nonce, and whether one can be
      // minted depends on session state that varies between the contract
      // harness and Playwright. This route only ever exists inside the test
      // blueprint, so a fixed header is accepted as well: the capability check
      // still stands for anything holding a real session.
      return $request->get_header('X-Hydra-Test') === 'seed'
        || current_user_can('edit_posts');
    },
    'callback' => function ($request) {
      global $wpdb;
      $documents = $request->get_json_params()['documents'] ?? array();

      // Roll the tables back, in-process, on the live connection.
      //
      // Rebuilding the fixture through wp_delete_post/wp_insert_post drags
      // hooks, meta, revisions and sanitisation behind every document, which is
      // what made a reset cost seconds. Copying the SQLite file instead is
      // fast but wrong here: WordPress keeps using $wpdb after this callback
      // returns, so closing the connection 500s the request, and deferring the
      // copy to shutdown corrupted state badly enough to fail 50 of 63 tests.
      //
      // This is what WP_UnitTestCase does in spirit — restore the baseline
      // rather than recreate it — done with direct SQL because the harness
      // drives WordPress over HTTP and cannot hold a transaction open across
      // requests.
      $baseline = get_option('hydra_test_baseline');
      $wanted = md5(wp_json_encode($documents));

      if (is_array($baseline) && ($baseline['hash'] ?? null) === $wanted) {
        $posts = $wpdb->posts;
        $meta = $wpdb->postmeta;

        // Everything the tests can touch: pages and the attachments they upload.
        $wpdb->query("DELETE FROM {$posts} WHERE post_type IN ('page','attachment')");

        foreach ($baseline['rows'] as $row) {
          $wpdb->insert($posts, $row);
        }
        $wpdb->query("DELETE FROM {$meta} WHERE post_id NOT IN (SELECT ID FROM {$posts})");

        // Uploads live on disk, not in the tables, so a restored database with
        // leftover files would let one asset test see the previous test's.
        $uploads = wp_upload_dir();
        if (!empty($uploads['basedir']) && is_dir($uploads['basedir'])) {
          $it = new RecursiveIteratorIterator(
            new RecursiveDirectoryIterator($uploads['basedir'], FilesystemIterator::SKIP_DOTS),
            RecursiveIteratorIterator::CHILD_FIRST
          );
          // FILES only, never the directories.
          //
          // What must not survive a reset is one test's uploaded
          // file being visible to the next. Removing the folders too
          // took away wp-content/uploads/<year>/<month>, which this
          // PHP-WASM build cannot recreate: every upload after the
          // first reset failed with
          //   rest_upload_sideload_error: Unable to create directory
          // reported to the caller as a bare 500 with no body.
          // Empty directories are harmless; missing ones are not.
          foreach ($it as $entry) {
            if (!$entry->isDir()) @unlink($entry->getPathname());
          }
        }

        wp_cache_flush();
        return array('ok' => true, 'restored' => true, 'count' => count($documents));
      }

      foreach (get_posts(array(
        'post_type' => 'page',
        'numberposts' => -1,
        'post_status' => 'any',
      )) as $existing) {
        wp_delete_post($existing->ID, true);
      }

      // Block markup is an HTML comment, and kses strips those for anyone
      // without unfiltered_html. Left on, every page seeds with empty content
      // and the blocks tests fail for a reason that has nothing to do with
      // blocks.
      kses_remove_filters();

      $id_by_path = array();
      foreach ($documents as $doc) {
        $segments = array_values(array_filter(explode('/', $doc['path'])));
        $parent_path = '/' . implode('/', array_slice($segments, 0, -1));
        $parent = count($segments) === 1 ? 0 : ($id_by_path[$parent_path] ?? 0);

        // DISTINCT post_modified per document. Inserting them all in one pass
        // gives every page the same timestamp to the second, and a sort by
        // last-edited then has nothing to order by: ascending and descending
        // come back in whatever order ties resolve, so a working sort is
        // indistinguishable from an ignored one.
        $offset = count($id_by_path);
        $stamp = gmdate('Y-m-d H:i:s', strtotime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + $offset * 60);

        $id = wp_insert_post(array(
          'post_type' => 'page',
          'post_title' => $doc['title'],
          'post_name' => $segments[count($segments) - 1],
          'post_parent' => $parent,
          'post_status' => $doc['state'] === 'published' ? 'publish' : 'draft',
          'post_content' => $doc['content'],
          'post_date' => $stamp,
          'post_date_gmt' => $stamp,
          'post_modified' => $stamp,
          'post_modified_gmt' => $stamp,
        ), true);

        if (is_wp_error($id)) {
          kses_init_filters();
          return new WP_Error('seed_failed', $doc['path'] . ': ' . $id->get_error_message());
        }
        $id_by_path[$doc['path']] = $id;
      }

      kses_init_filters();

      // Record the baseline the rollback restores to. Stored WITH the fixture's
      // hash, so editing seed.json rebuilds instead of silently restoring
      // yesterday's content.
      $rows = $wpdb->get_results(
        "SELECT ID, post_author, post_date, post_date_gmt, post_content, post_title,"
        . " post_excerpt, post_status, comment_status, ping_status, post_password,"
        . " post_name, post_modified, post_modified_gmt, post_parent, guid, menu_order,"
        . " post_type, post_mime_type"
        . " FROM {$wpdb->posts} WHERE post_type IN ('page','attachment')",
        ARRAY_A
      );
      update_option('hydra_test_baseline', array('hash' => $wanted, 'rows' => $rows), false);

      return array('ok' => true, 'restored' => false, 'count' => count($documents));
    },
  ));
});

<?php
/**
 * Let the bridge's adapter talk to WordPress from the iframe.
 *
 * The contract suite runs the adapter under node, where same-origin policy does
 * not exist. The journey runs the SAME adapter inside the iframe, served from
 * the test frontend's origin, so every CMS call is cross-origin and
 * credentialled — and vanilla WordPress sends no CORS headers at all, so the
 * adapter failed to register with a bare "TypeError: Failed to fetch".
 *
 * The Origin is REFLECTED rather than '*': the requests carry cookies, and a
 * wildcard is rejected by the browser for credentialled requests.
 *
 * Content-Disposition is allowed because asset.upload sends the filename
 * in it; leaving it out failed the PREFLIGHT, so the upload surfaced as a
 * bare "Failed to fetch" and every request after it timed out.
 *
 * X-WP-Total is exposed because the adapter reads collection sizes from it;
 * without that the header is invisible to script and every total reads as 0.
 */
add_action('init', function () {
  $origin = isset($_SERVER['HTTP_ORIGIN']) ? $_SERVER['HTTP_ORIGIN'] : '';
  if ($origin !== '') {
    header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin: ' . $origin);
    header('Vary: Origin');
    header('Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true');
    header('Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS');
    header('Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Content-Disposition, X-WP-Nonce, X-Hydra-Test, Authorization');
    header('Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-WP-Total, X-WP-TotalPages, Location');
  }
  // Answer only a REAL preflight. A bare OPTIONS is a legitimate REST call —
  // types.getSchema fetches the field schema with one — and short-circuiting
  // every OPTIONS returned an empty 200 for it, which broke two contract tests
  // that had nothing to do with CORS.
  if (
    isset($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'])
    && $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] === 'OPTIONS'
    && isset($_SERVER['HTTP_ACCESS_CONTROL_REQUEST_METHOD'])
  ) {
    status_header(200);
    exit;
  }
}, 0);

<?php
/**
 * Allow application passwords over plain http, for tests only.
 *
 * WordPress gates the application-password flow behind HTTPS
 * (wp_is_application_passwords_available), so on a local http Playground
 * `wp-admin/authorize-application.php` 501s and the flow cannot run at all.
 *
 * This enables the REAL core feature rather than faking identity. It replaces
 * a determine_current_user filter that treated every request as the admin,
 * which made the suite pass while testing none of the authentication the
 * design depends on. A production install has HTTPS and needs none of this.
 */
add_filter('wp_is_application_passwords_available', '__return_true');
